card: Paper card. Question: Can high-entropy effects be utilized to induce a significant glass-to-glass transition in metallic glasses, and what are the structural and thermodynamic mechanisms behind this phenomenon?. System: Equiatomic NbNiZrTiCo high-entropy metallic glass (HEMG), with comparative systems NbNiZrTiCu and NbNiZrTiCoCu. Processing: Arc melting of pure elements (Nb, Ni, Zr, Ti, Co, Cu; purity ≥ 99.9 wt.%) under high-purity argon, followed by remelting five times; ribbon production via melt-spinning at a wheel surface velocity of 32 m s−1; heat treatment by heating to 855 K (TA) at 20 K min−1 and cooling at 20 K min−1. Test conditions: Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) at heating rates of 10–50 K min−1 and Flash DSC at >1000 K s−1; in-situ synchrotron X-ray diffraction from 305 K to 803 K at 30 K min−1; nanoindentation; dynamic mechanical analysis (DMA); atom probe tomography (APT) at 65 K; high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) at 200 kV. Findings: The as-prepared NbNiZrTiCo HEMG exhibits an enormous exothermic peak at 781 K with a heat release of 1.65 kJ mol−1, which is approximately 130% of the subsequent crystallization exotherm (1.27 kJ mol−1).; The glass-to-glass transition is irreversible; the heat-treated sample shows a distinct glass transition temperature (Tg) at ~764 K and lacks the first exothermic peak observed in the as-prepared state.; Nanoindentation measurements reveal a drastic increase in hardness from 6.78 GPa to 9.46 GPa (approximately 40% increase) after the transition.; In-situ synchrotron X-ray diffraction shows a significant non-linear shift of the first peak in the total structure function S(Q) and a narrowing of the full width at half maximum (FWHM) during the transition.; Pair-distribution function (G(r)) analysis indicates a contraction of short-range atomic distances (r11 and r12 shift to low-r) and prominent splitting of the second peak, signifying enhanced short- and medium-range ordering.; Atom probe tomography confirms a uniform element distribution at the sub-nanometer scale in both as-prepared and heat-treated samples, excluding spinodal decomposition.; The calculated lower limit of entropy change (ΔSH−L) for the transition is −1.96 J mol−1 K−1, with a corresponding enthalpy change (ΔHH−L) of −1.65 kJ mol−1.; Substituting Co with Cu to form NbNiZrTiCu (maintaining high excess configurational entropy) and adding Cu to form NbNiZrTiCoCu both result in similar glass-to-glass transitions.. Mechanism: The authors propose that the high configurational entropy (SC) and high excess configurational entropy (SE) dynamically stabilize a high-energy glass state during rapid vitrification by hindering atomic reconstruction and slowing diffusion. Upon heating, this high-energy state undergoes a thermodynamically driven transition to a low-energy, more ordered glass state, releasing a large amount of heat. The transition is driven by the specific combination of high SC and high SE (related to atomic size misfit), which enables the formation of a high-energy glass that is distinct from conventional metallic glasses.. Limitations: The text notes that the observed phase transition is an irreversible process, meaning the calculated entropy change represents a lower limit. Additionally, the detailed structural changes cannot be fully resolved by atom probe tomography due to its limited spatial resolution, and some weak diffraction peaks in crystallized samples could not be identified.. Future work: The authors suggest that the HEMGs may serve as model materials for exploring glass-to-glass transitions and the fundamental nature of glasses in materials science and condensed-matter physics. They also propose potential applications as energetic materials due to the large anomalous exotherm, which could contribute to combustion heats and lower ignition temperatures.. Quote: "An unusual glass-to-glass phase transition is discovered during heating with an enormous heat release even larger than that of the following crystallization at higher temperatures."

card: Paper card. Question: Can configurational entropy be engineered to stabilize a single-phase solid solution in a five-component oxide system where the constituent binary oxides do not form solid solutions, and can this transition be reversed?. System: Equimolar mixture of MgO, CoO, NiO, CuO, and ZnO (labeled E1). Processing: Solid-state synthesis: powders milled for 2 h, pressed into pellets at 31,000 N, fired in air at temperatures ranging from 700 to 1,100 °C with 50 °C increments, and quenched; thin films prepared via pulsed laser deposition at 600 °C with 3 J cm⁻² energy density.. Test conditions: X-ray diffraction (XRD) monitoring phase evolution from 700 to 1,100 °C; differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) and in situ XRD at 5 °C min⁻¹; EXAFS at Advanced Photon Source 12-BM-B; STEM-EDS analysis at 200 kV.. Findings: Full conversion to a single-phase rocksalt structure occurs between 850 and 900 °C, with no additional peaks observed above this range.; Removing any single component from the five-component mixture results in a multiphase material when equilibrated at 875 °C for 12 h.; Deviations from equimolarity by ±2, ±6, and ±10% increase the transition temperature to single phase, confirming the entropic driving force.; The phase transformation from multiphase to single phase is endothermic, with a measured enthalpy change of approximately 12 kJ mol⁻¹ (±2 kJ mol⁻¹).; EXAFS data shows cation-to-anion first-neighbour distances are identical within ±0.01 Å for Zn, Ni, Cu, and Co, consistent with random distribution.; STEM-EDS mapping reveals chemically and structurally homogeneous material with no evidence of phase separation or clustering at the atomic scale.; A small mass loss of approximately 1.5% occurs at the transition due to the reduction of 3+ to 2+ cations during the conversion of spinel intermediates to rocksalt.. Mechanism: The authors argue that the high configurational entropy of the five-component equimolar mixture overcomes the positive enthalpic penalties associated with structural transitions (specifically for CuO and ZnO) and mixing, stabilizing the single-phase solid solution at elevated temperatures. The entropy term (TΔS) in the Gibbs free energy becomes dominant, driving the reversible transition from a multiphase state to a random solid solution where cations occupy a single sublattice homogeneously.. Limitations: The authors note that quantitative calorimetry presents challenges, and the assumption of ideal mixing for enthalpy calculations is a simplification; literature reports indicate finite and mixed-sign enthalpies of mixing that are not fully captured by the reference transition enthalpy values.. Future work: The authors propose that entropic stabilization should be explored in other systems with intermediate anions, such as chalcogenides, nitrides, and halides, particularly where covalent character is modest, and call for rigorous theoretical exploration of the crystallographic model where intermediate anions render cation sites energetically equivalent.. Quote: "entropy predominates the thermodynamic landscape, and drives a reversible solid-state transformation between a multiphase and single-phase state."

card: Paper card. Question: How can high-entropy alloys (HEAs) and high-entropy oxides (HEOs) be synthesized and applied as protective layers for interconnectors and anode components in hydrocarbon-fueled solid oxide fuel cells (SOFCs) to overcome issues like chromium evaporation and carbon deposition?. System: FeCoNiMnCu high-entropy alloy coating converted to (FeCoNiMnCu)3O4 spinel; HEA/GDC anode catalyst containing Ni, Co, Cu, Fe, Mn on Gd-doped CeO2 (GDC) support. Processing: Vacuum induction melting to create sputtering target; magnetron sputtering deposition of 4 μm coating on SUS 430 steel at 200 °C for 2 h (1.2 kW power, 0.13 Pa Ar); thermal conversion at 800 °C for 10 weeks (1680 h total); co-precipitation of HEA from nitrate precursors with citric acid, calcination at 500 °C for 6 h, mixing with GDC (65:35 wt ratio). Test conditions: Oxidation in air at 800 °C for up to 10 weeks; SOFC cell testing at 750 °C; Steam reforming of methane (SRM) in fixed-bed tube reactor at 700–800 °C with GHSV of 45,000 1/h. Findings: After 10 weeks of oxidation at 800 °C, the FeCoNiMnCu coating converted to a uniform (FeCoNiMnCu)3O4 spinel layer with a surface Cr concentration of only 4.34%.; The area-specific resistance (ASR) of the oxidized HEA coating decreased from 8.21 mΩ·cm² after 1 week to 6.59 mΩ·cm² after 10 weeks at 800 °C.; The ASR of the scale was 17 mΩ·cm² at 600 °C, which is well below the accepted limit of 0.1 Ω·cm².; The HEA/GDC catalyst showed excellent stability during SRM, whereas Ni/YSZ and Ni/GDC catalysts rapidly degraded with time.; After 30 h of SOFC cell testing, the post-test HEA/GDC anode layer was carbon-free, while the Ni/YSZ anode contained 17.3% carbon.; The reforming rate of the HEA/GDC catalyst increased from 27% at 700 °C to 42% at 800 °C.; A current density of approximately 100 mA/cm² was achieved at 750 °C in the SOFC cell test using the HEA/GDC anode.. Mechanism: The high-entropy spinel coating thermally converted from the HEA effectively blocks chromium out-diffusion from the substrate, reducing the growth of the Cr-rich oxide layer and lowering electrical resistivity. The HEA-based anode demonstrates superior carbon resistance because the mingled sites of multiple transition metals prevent the deposition and fiber growth of carbon that typically damages Ni-based anodes.. Limitations: The conductivity of the (FeCoNiMnCu)3O4 spinel was not measured directly in the study; the reforming rate of the HEA/GDC catalyst was lower than that of the Ni-based catalysts at 750 °C.. Future work: Further study and development of carbon-resistant anodes for hydrocarbon-fueled SOFCs with direct internal reforming is needed based on the promising results.. Quote: "The coating of 4 μm in thickness was deposited on the SUS 430 steel substrate under sputtering power of 1.2 kW for 2 h at 200 °C in a chamber with an Ar pressure of 0.13 Pa."

Paper card. Question: How does high configurational entropy and multi-cation doping affect the ionic conductivity, activation energy, and structural stability of fluorite- and pyrochlore-structured high-entropy oxides (HEOs) compared to conventional SOFC electrolytes like YSZ and GDC?. System: Fluorite-structured HEOs: (Hf0.25Zr0.25Ce0.25Y0.25)O2-δ (HEFO1), (Hf0.2Zr0.2Ce0.2)(Y0.2Yb0.2)O2-δ (HEF04B), (Hf0.327Ce0.456Zr0.217)0.85Yb0.15O1.93 (Yb-15(1)); Pyrochlore-structured HEOs: (Nd0.2Sm0.2Gd0.2Dy0.2Y0.2)2Zr2O7 (HEC-1 to HEC-5); Ceria-based HEOs: CeGdDySmPrO2-δ, CeGdLaSmPrO2-δ. Processing: High-energy ball milling followed by spark plasma sintering and annealing in air at 1500 °C with furnace cooling (50 °C/min); Solid-state reaction method with final sintering at 1500–1700 °C; Sol-gel method followed by compaction and free sintering at 1500 °C in air. Test conditions: Electrical conductivity measured in dry air in the temperature range of 650–850 °C; Conductivity measured at 600 °C and 800 °C; Activation energy determined in temperature ranges of 300–750 °C and 170–560 °C. Findings: Conductivity of fluorite HEOs (e.g., HEFO1) at 850 °C ranged from 1.9 to 2.9 mS/cm, significantly lower than the 30 mS/cm observed for YSZ.; Activation energies for HEO fluorites were 1.14–1.29 eV, higher than the 1.0 eV for YSZ.; The highest conductivity for ZrO2-based HEOs (CCFO2) was 5.35 × 10−4 S/cm at 600 °C with an activation energy of 0.66 eV.; Pyrochlore HEC-5 achieved a conductivity of 7.1 × 10−3 S/cm at 800 °C, higher than base low and medium zirconates.; Ceria-based HEOs (CeGdLaSmPrO2-δ) reached 0.001 S/cm at 510 °C with activation energies of 0.52–0.53 eV.; Increasing the cation radius ratio r(A3+)/r(B4+) in pyrochlore HEOs increased conductivity due to higher mobile vacancy concentration.; Raman spectroscopy showed a blue shift in the main band for HEOs, indicating lattice compression, and an increase in the 570 cm−1 band intensity indicating more oxygen vacancies.. Mechanism: The authors argue that ionic conductivity in HEOs is inhibited by local crystal lattice distortion caused by relatively high ionic radius differences (δrion), which lowers oxygen mobility. Additionally, high deviation of oxygen non-stoichiometry from the optimal 4% value leads to defect association, reducing free charge carriers. In pyrochlore structures, higher conductivity is ensured by a continuous and energetically favorable pathway for oxygen jumps between 48f-sites, which cannot form in fluorite structures due to random cation/anion occupation.. Limitations: The high cost and limited resources of scandium and gallium in alternative electrolytes; poor chemical stability of Bi2O3-based electrolytes in reducing atmospheres; reduction of Ce4+ to Ce3+ in doped ceria under anode conditions causing power efficiency loss; difficulty in stabilizing fluorite HEOs without deterioration of transport properties; low conductivity of HEOs compared to conventional electrolytes in many cases.. Future work: Further efforts should be applied to the search for new methods to stabilize fluorite HEOs without deterioration of their transport properties; HEOs with pyrochlore structure are highly stable and entropy disordering enhances transport properties, providing a point for future development; HEO proton and dual conductors with perovskite structure are highly demanded.. Quote: "The authors argue that decreasing the conductivity may be related to a smaller gran size of HE ceramics as well as to a high doping level, exceeding the optimal value for the ZrO2-based ceramic equal to 8–10 mol.%"

card: Paper card. Question: How can shifting alloy design from single-phase equiatomic to dual- or multiphase non-equiatomic configurations with controlled phase instability enable the joint activation of multiple strengthening and toughening mechanisms to achieve superior strength–ductility combinations?. System: 3d transition-metal non-equiatomic HEAs including Fe80−xMnxCo10Cr10 (x = 30–45 at.%), Co20Cr20Fe40−yMn20Niy (y = 0–20 at.%), and interstitially alloyed variants like Fe49.5Mn30Co10Cr10C0.5. Processing: Vacuum induction melting followed by hot-rolling at 900°C with 50% thickness reduction, homogenization at 1200°C for >2 h with water quenching, cold-rolling to ~60% reduction, and annealing at 900°C for 3–60 min to control grain size and phase fractions. Test conditions: Room temperature tensile testing; microstructural characterization via XRD, EBSD, ECCI, APT, and TEM; thermodynamic calculations using Calphad at 300 K. Findings: The Fe50Mn30Co10Cr10 dual-phase alloy exhibits significantly higher strength and ductility than single-phase variants due to the TRIP effect and massive solid-solution strengthening.; Adding 0.5 at.% carbon to Fe50Mn30Co10Cr10 yields Fe49.5Mn30Co10Cr10C0.5 with ultimate tensile strength up to nearly 1 GPa and total elongation of ~60%.; The interstitially alloyed Fe49.5Mn30Co10Cr10C0.5 shows twice the tensile strength of the equiatomic Co20Cr20Fe20Mn20Ni20 reference while maintaining identical ductility.; In Fe50Mn30Co10Cr10, annealing at 900°C for 60 min increases FCC grain size from ~4.5 μm to ~17.5 μm and causes nonmonotonic variation of HCP phase fraction (dropping to ~14% then rising to ~36%).; Compositional inhomogeneity in as-cast or non-homogenized alloys reduces ductility and strain hardening due to localized phase transformation in Fe-enriched regions.; The Fe40Mn40Co10Cr10 single-phase alloy achieves ~95 MPa higher ultimate strength than the equiatomic Co20Cr20Fe20Mn20Ni20 alloy due to enhanced twinning behavior.; The Fe49.5Mn30Co10Cr10C0.5 alloy contains M23C6 carbide nanoparticles with average size 50–100 nm and volume fraction ~1.5 vol.%.. Mechanism: The authors argue that tuning the free energy difference between FCC and HCP phases via non-equiatomic composition and interstitial addition controls stacking fault energy, enabling sequential activation of deformation mechanisms (dislocation slip, TWIP, TRIP, precipitation, grain boundary strengthening) which collectively enhance strain-hardening capacity and strength–ductility synergy.. Limitations: High-Mn alloys (>10 at.%) retain Mn-enriched inclusions even after long-term homogenization; long-term annealing at intermediate temperatures can cause chemical segregation; the study focuses primarily on room temperature properties without data on low or elevated temperatures.. Future work: The authors propose investigating strength–ductility at low and elevated temperatures, exploring multifunctionalities (corrosion, fatigue, magnetic, hydrogen resistance), introducing shape-memory effects via phase stability design, developing refractory non-equiatomic HEAs (Ti, Nb, Ta, Zr, Hf, V, Mo, W), and screening minor interstitial elements (C, N, B, O) for further performance enhancement.. Quote: "This design direction provides ample possibilities for joint activation of a number of strengthening and toughening mechanisms."

card: Paper card. Question: How can non-equiatomic medium-entropy alloys be designed to achieve novel two-phase microstructures, and can existing parametric phase formation rules predict the phase separation behaviors in these alloys?. System: Co-free Fex(CrNiAl)100−x (at.%, x = 25, 35, 45, 55, 65) medium-entropy alloys. Processing: Vacuum arc-melting under argon protection with electromagnetic stirring five times, followed by natural cooling in the furnace. Test conditions: Room temperature characterization using X-ray diffractometer (Cu radiation, 2θ: 20°–100°), scanning electron microscopy, and transmission electron microscopy with high-angle annular dark-field detector and energy dispersive spectrometry. Findings: The alloys exhibit novel two-phase microstructures consisting of B2-ordered nanoprecipitates and BCC-disordered matrix.; As the Fe content (x) increases from 25 to 65, the nanoprecipitate structure transfers from a spinodal-like intertwined structure to a nanoparticle dispersed structure.; In the Fe25 alloy, the Ni-Al-rich and Fe-Cr-rich phases alternate with a period of about 200 nm in width.; The average size of nanoparticles decreases with increasing Fe content: ~400 nm in Fe35, ~250 nm in Fe45, ~200 nm in Fe55, and ~100 nm in Fe65.; The Fe55 and Fe65 alloys contain a large density of highly dispersed nanoparticles in the matrix.; Previous parametric approaches (atomic size difference δ, mixing enthalpy ΔHmix, mixing entropy ΔSmix, valence electron concentration VEC, and parameter Ω) are unable to describe the phase separation behaviors observed.; The VEC values for the alloys range between 6.75 and 7.42, yet only BCC and B2 phases form, contradicting the VEC rule that predicts FCC phase stability for VEC ≥ 8.. Mechanism: Phase separation is driven by thermodynamic factors where Ni and Al have the most negative mixing enthalpy and largest electronegativity difference, favoring the formation of Ni-Al-rich B2 phases; Fe is thermodynamically favored to dissolve in the B2 phase, while Cr stays in the matrix forming the BCC phase due to smaller electronegativity difference with Al. The morphology (intertwined vs. dispersed) is controlled by the concentration of Ni and Al elements.. Limitations: The detailed formation processes of the Ni-Al-rich precipitates in the Fex(CrNiAl)100−x alloys are still unclear.. Future work: The detailed formation processes of the Ni-Al-rich precipitates will be studied in the future.. Quote: "Here we propose a novel design of non-equiatomic medium-entropy alloys that contain one matrix element and several equiatomic alloying elements."

card: Paper card. Question: How can uniformly dispersed high-entropy alloy nanoparticles (HEA-NPs) be synthesized on granular supports (e.g., carbon, Al2O3, zeolite) without phase separation, overcoming the limitations of conventional fixed-bed pyrolysis?. System: Denary (MnCoNiCuRhPdSnIrPtAu), quinary (FeCoPdIrPt, CuPdSnPtAu), and other multi-element (up to 10 elements) HEA-NPs supported on graphene oxide (GO), carbon black, γ-Al2O3, and zeolite (Permutit). Processing: Fast moving bed pyrolysis (FMBP) following wet impregnation: Metal chlorides coordinated with 1,10-Phenanthroline loaded on supports; quartz boat pushed into a 923 K furnace zone at 20 cm s−1 (reaching 923 K within 5 s); annealing for 120 min at 923 K under Ar (100 sccm) or H2 (100 sccm) for oxide supports. Test conditions: Electrochemical hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) in 1 M KOH (pH 13.8) at 10 mA cm−2 and 100 mA cm−2; stability tested via chronopotentiometry for 150 h; structural characterization via HR-STEM, HAADF-STEM, EDX, XRD, XPS, and ICP-OES. Findings: HEA-NPs achieved a narrow size distribution of ~2 nm up to denary compositions at 923 K; FMBP ensures simultaneous pyrolysis of mixed precursors, preventing phase separation unlike fixed-bed pyrolysis (FBP) which yields phase-separated alloys; FeCoPdIrPt@GO exhibited an overpotential of 42 mV at 10 mA cm−2, lower than commercial Pt/C (64 mV); Mass activity of FeCoPdIrPt@GO at 100 mV overpotential was 9.1 mA μgPt, 26 times higher than Pt/C (0.35 mA μgPt); Long-term stability of 150 h maintained at 10 mA cm−2 with no obvious change in morphology or composition; Atomic ratio error in synthesized alloys was below 15%, confirmed by EDX and ICP-OES; Tafel slope for FeCoPdIrPt was 82 mV dec−1, indicating the fastest kinetics among tested samples. Mechanism: The rapid heating to 923 K within 5 s creates high supersaturation of monomers, leading to a small critical nucleus radius (r* = 0.313 nm) and low critical excess free energy (ΔGr* = 2.54 × 10−20 J). This thermodynamically favors the formation of small, homogeneous nuclei clusters without phase separation, whereas slower heating (FBP/SMBP) results in larger nuclei and phase segregation due to higher ΔGr*.. Limitations: The text notes that HEA-NPs with low loading (3 wt%) were too small for clear EDX mapping, requiring higher loading (10 wt%) for elemental analysis; also, annealing times of 30 min led to carbon wrapping, while 180 min caused significant particle growth.. Future work: The authors propose a scalable method for production of supported HEA-NPs and suggest the strategy opens a venue for synthesizing alloys with tunable compositions for applications in catalysis, chemical sensing, biology, and energy conversion.. Quote: "Fast moving bed pyrolysis strategy ensures the mixed metal precursors rapidly and simultaneously pyrolyzed at high temperatures, resulting in nuclei with a small size."

card: Paper card. Question: How does the presence of local chemical order (LCO) influence the formation, evolution, and recombination of irradiation-induced point defects and defect clusters in equiatomic CrCoNi medium-entropy alloys compared to a random solid solution?. System: Equiatomic CrCoNi medium-entropy alloy (MEA) in two states: water-quenched (approximated as a random solid solution, RSS) and aged at 1,000 °C for 120 h (LCO CrCoNi); pure Ni used as a benchmark.. Processing: Raw ingot homogenized at 1,200 °C for 48 h; split into two treatments: (1) water quenched to room temperature to form RSS; (2) aged at 1,000 °C for 120 h followed by slow furnace cooling to induce LCO. Ion irradiation performed in situ at 300 K using 50 keV He+ ions. Atomistic simulations prepared RSS by random distribution and LCO via MD/MC at 1,300 K with variance-constrained semigrand canonical ensemble.. Test conditions: In situ TEM irradiation at 300 K with 50 keV He+ ions up to 1.0 dpa; MD simulations of primary damage with PKA energies of 5, 10, 20, and 40 keV; diffusion simulations at various temperatures (including 1,200 K) to measure vacancy and interstitial mobility.. Findings: The areal fraction of LCO regions is approximately 3% in water-quenched RSS CrCoNi versus ~30% in the 1,000 °C-aged LCO CrCoNi.; At a low irradiation dose of 0.16 dpa, the LCO sample is nearly defect-free while the RSS sample already contains visible defect clusters.; The number density of defect clusters in the LCO sample is significantly smaller than in the RSS sample across the entire dose range of 0.16 to 1.0 dpa.; The average activation energy for interstitial diffusion increases from 0.22 eV in RSS to 0.34 eV in LCO, while for vacancies it increases from 0.69 eV to 0.76 eV.; The difference in activation energy between interstitial and vacancy diffusion narrows from 0.47 eV in RSS to 0.42 eV in LCO, reducing the mobility ratio.; The correlation factor for interstitial diffusion decreases by 29% (from 0.232 to 0.165) in LCO compared to RSS, indicating stronger localization of interstitial motion.; Large-sized defect clusters (Ncluster > 30) are suppressed in LCO CrCoNi, with the number of point defects in large clusters being ~35% lower than in RSS.; The recombination rate of Frenkel pairs at the end of the thermal spike is nearly identical for RSS and LCO (~99.6%), but the LCO sample retains fewer surviving FPs due to enhanced recombination during the cooling phase.. Mechanism: The authors argue that LCO enhances irradiation resistance through a two-pronged kinetic effect: (1) it increases migration energy barriers, slowing down the diffusion of both vacancies and interstitials (localizing their motion); and (2) it narrows the mobility ratio between interstitials and vacancies (by affecting interstitials more strongly), which increases the probability of their recombination and annihilation during the cooling phase of the collision cascade, thereby reducing the number of surviving defects and large clusters.. Limitations: The study notes that small-sized defect clusters (Ncluster < 8) are not detectable by in-situ TEM due to resolution limits and are susceptible to dissolution, so the comparison between experiment and simulation focuses on large-sized clusters. The extent of LCO investigated is limited to chemical short-range order (CSRO) developed via the specific aging treatment.. Future work: The authors propose that tailoring composition and heat treatment to extend LCO beyond CSRO into medium-range or long-range order, or adding interstitial alloying elements (such as C, N) with chemical affinity for specific constituents, could further boost irradiation tolerance.. Quote: "increased local chemical order (e.g., via thermal aging) significantly enhances their resistance to irradiation damage by narrowing the mobility ratio of irradiation-induced interstitials and vacancies that can facilitate their recombination."

card: Paper card. Question: How do the strength, ductility, and fracture toughness of an equiatomic CrCoNi medium-entropy alloy compare to high-entropy alloys and conventional materials, particularly at cryogenic temperatures, and what mechanisms drive these properties?. System: Equiatomic CrCoNi medium-entropy alloy (MEA). Processing: Arc-melted high-purity elements (>99.9%) under argon, drop-cast into copper moulds, homogenized at 1,200 °C for 24 h, cold-forged and cross-rolled to ~10 mm thickness (60% reduction), then annealed at 800 °C for 1 h in air to achieve a recrystallized microstructure with 5–50 μm grains.. Test conditions: Uniaxial tensile tests at 293 K, 198 K, and 77 K with a strain rate of 10⁻³ s⁻¹; Compact-tension (C(T)) fracture toughness tests at 293 K, 198 K, and 77 K with fatigue pre-cracking and side-grooving per ASTM E1820.. Findings: At 77 K, yield strength reached 657 MPa and ultimate tensile strength reached 1,311 MPa, representing a ~50% increase from room temperature.; Tensile ductility (failure strain) increased to ~0.9 (90%) at 77 K, a ~25% increase from room temperature.; Fracture toughness (KJIc) at crack initiation increased from 208 MPa m1/2 at 293 K to 273 MPa m1/2 at 77 K.; Crack-growth toughness at 77 K reached critical stress-intensity values of ~430 MPa m1/2 (J ~900 kJ m⁻²).; The alloy exhibited a high strain-hardening exponent (n) of 0.4 at cryogenic temperatures.; The CrCoNi alloy showed ~15% higher tensile strength, ~30% higher ductility, and ~50% higher work of fracture than the five-component CrMnFeCoNi alloy at room temperature.; At 77 K, the CrCoNi alloy displayed ~25% higher KJIc, ~27% higher ductility, and ~31% higher work of fracture compared to the CrMnFeCoNi alloy.. Mechanism: The exceptional damage tolerance results from continuous steady strain hardening that suppresses plastic instability, driven by pronounced dislocation activity and deformation-induced nano-twinning. Nano-twinning acts as a dominant deformation mode that provides a steady source of strain hardening, delaying necking and accommodating strain, with its intensity increasing as temperature decreases from room temperature to 77 K.. Limitations: The yield strength at 77 K was slightly lower than the CrMnFeCoNi alloy, attributed to the non-uniform grain size of the current material; the volume fraction of void-initiating inclusions was not accurately quantified relative to the five-component alloy.. Future work: Further studies are needed to accurately determine the relative volume fractions of void-initiating inclusions in the MEA and HEA and to identify their chemistry and crystal structure by TEM after extraction from the voids.. Quote: "strength, ductility and toughness of the CrCoNi alloy improve to strength levels above 1.3 GPa, failure strains up to 90% and KJIc values of 275 MPa m1/2."

card: Paper card. Question: How does increasing chemical disorder and compositional complexity in single-phase concentrated solid solution alloys (SP-CSAs) affect energy dissipation pathways and subsequent defect evolution under ion irradiation?. System: Single-phase fcc concentrated solid solution alloys: elemental Nickel (Ni), binary NiCo, binary NiFe, and quaternary NiCoFeCr (all equiatomic), plus non-equiatomic Ni0.65Fe0.35 and Ni0.40Fe0.60.. Processing: High-purity elemental metals arc melted and drop cast into copper moulds; single crystals directionally solidified in an optical floating zone furnace under Ar atmosphere; polished to damage-free surfaces for ion channelling.. Test conditions: Room temperature irradiation using 3 MeV Au2+ ions (fluence 1-2 × 10^13 cm^-2) and 1.5 MeV Ni+ ions (fluence 6 × 10^13 to 2 × 10^14 cm^-2); electrical resistivity measured between 5 K and 300 K; thermal conductivity measured at room temperature; in situ ion channelling and high-resolution TEM characterization.. Findings: Electrical resistivity at 5 K increases from ~0.1 μΩ cm for Ni to 77.1 μΩ cm for NiCoFeCr, indicating a substantial reduction in electron mean free path.; Total thermal conductivity at 300 K decreases from 88 W m−1 K−1 for Ni to 12.8 W m−1 K−1 for NiCoFeCr.; Backscattering yield (damage indicator) for NiFe is approximately half that of pure Ni after 3 MeV Au irradiation.; Stable defect production in NiFe is ~2 times lower than in pure Ni according to molecular dynamics cascade simulations.; Quaternary NiCoFeCr shows ~5 times less accumulated damage than pure Ni under Ni ion irradiation.; Increasing Fe concentration from 35% to 60% in Ni-Fe alloys enhances irradiation resistance.; Stacking fault tetrahedra (SFT) sizes are smaller in alloys (4.3-4.4 nm) compared to pure Ni (7.0 nm) due to slower defect migration.. Mechanism: Chemical disorder in SP-CSAs causes significant smearing of the electronic band structure (Bloch spectral function), reducing the electron mean free path and drastically lowering electronic thermal conductivity. This leads to less efficient heat dissipation, prolonging the lifetime of thermal spikes generated by ion collisions. The extended thermal spike duration and localized energy deposition alter defect energetics, increasing migration barriers and formation energies, which suppresses the clustering of point defects into larger, deleterious structures.. Limitations: The study focuses on simple fcc lattice structures and early-stage defect dynamics; the authors note that the results should not be interpreted as HEAs being intrinsically more radiation resistant in all cases, but rather that complexity is a tunable parameter for modifying transport properties.. Future work: The authors propose further exploration to understand how chemistry and composition can alter energy dissipation mechanisms to drive self-recovery from damage states, aiming to design radiation-resistant alloys by controlling coupling strengths and defect energetics at the atomic and electronic levels.. Quote: "much slower energy dissipation results in less deleterious defects and consequent slower damage accumulation under ion irradiation."

card: Paper card. Question: How can the strength–ductility trade-off inherent to traditional alloys be overcome in multi-principal-element alloys by exploiting multiple levels of heterogeneities?. System: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) and medium-entropy alloys (MEAs) including FCC-based systems (e.g., CoCrFeNi, CrCoNi, VCoNi), BCC-based refractory systems (e.g., TiZrHfNbTa), dual-phase eutectic lamella HEAs, and alloys with multicomponent intermetallic nanoparticles (MCINPs). Processing: Partial recrystallization to create heterogeneous grain structures (HGS), spinodal decomposition to form precipitates, addition of oxygen solutes (~2 at%) to form nanoscale complexes, and intentional alloying to tune stacking fault energy (SFE) for deformation-induced transformations. Test conditions: Room temperature (RT) uniaxial tensile testing; cryogenic temperatures (77 K and 4 K) for specific FCC MEAs; compression testing for some refractory BCC HEAs. Findings: An FCC-MCINP alloy achieved a yield strength above 1 GPa with a uniform elongation (εu) of ~50%, showing no strength–ductility trade-off compared to unstrengthened elemental metals.; A single-phase CrCoNi MEA with a heterogeneous grain structure (HGS) spanning nano-to-micro scales reached a gigapascal yield strength while maintaining εu in excess of 20%.; The VCoNi MEA achieved near-GPa yield strength with εu ~30% and total elongation ~38%, attributed to maximized lattice friction from atomic size mismatch.; In BCC-TiZrHfNb HEA, adding ~2 at% oxygen formed nanoscale (O, Ti, Zr)-complexes that increased tensile elongation from ~14% to ~28% while maintaining high strength.; Stress-assisted martensitic transformation in BCC-Ti35Zr27.5Hf27.5Nb5Ta5 HEA created a 65% volume fraction of internally twinned martensite, doubling the strain-hardening rate.; Wide hysteresis loops in load–unload–reload stress–strain curves demonstrated that nonhomogeneous plastic deformation in HGS alloys imparts high back stresses contributing to strain hardening.; At cryogenic temperatures (77 K and 4 K), the CrCoNi MEA exhibited strain-hardening rates and εu comparable to the best 316 austenitic stainless steels due to reduced dynamic recovery.. Mechanism: The authors argue that the high concentration of multiple principal elements creates a rugged energy landscape with statistical fluctuations in composition and local chemical order (LCO), causing dislocations to adopt a wavy line and face intermittent 'nanoscale segment detrapping' barriers. This intrinsic lattice friction is compounded by a hierarchy of heterogeneities (defects, precipitates, grain boundaries, phase boundaries) that promote nonhomogeneous plastic deformation, geometrically necessary dislocation storage, and dynamic mechanisms like twinning (TWIP) and transformation (TRIP), which sustain high strain-hardening rates to delay necking.. Limitations: Refractory BCC HEAs often lack room-temperature tensile ductility due to a drastic rise in the ductile-to-brittle transition temperature; TRIP-assisted DP alloys with low initial yield strength require hardening (e.g., cold work) which causes the strain-hardening rate to become inadequate, restoring the strength–ductility trade-off at high σy levels.. Future work: Continued endeavors to tailor heterogeneities to ward off plastic instabilities and realize even better strength–ductility balance, expanding the repertoire of alloys in compositions and properties through refined and enhanced HEAs.. Quote: "The strength of HEAs is considerably higher than traditional solid solutions, as the many constituents lead to a rugged energy landscape that increases the resistance to dislocation motion."

card: Paper card. Question: How can morphology and surface chemistry be engineered to create inexpensive electrocatalysts that maintain high activity and stability for the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) across a wide pH range at high current densities?. System: Flat platinum foil, molybdenum disulfide (MoS2) microspheres composed of radially aligned nanosheets, and MoS2 microspheres decorated with molybdenum carbide (Mo2C) nanoparticles (MoS2/Mo2C). Processing: Two-step synthesis: (1) Hydrothermal growth of MoS2 microspheres on Ti foil at 180 °C for 24 h; (2) Chemical vapor deposition (CVD) at 750 °C for 20–100 min using Ar/H2/CH4 (100/30/10 sccm) to convert MoS2 edges to Mo2C nanoparticles. Test conditions: Electrochemical testing in 1.0 M KOH (alkaline) and 0.5 M H2SO4 (acidic) electrolytes; current densities up to 1000 mA cm−2; 24 h stability tests; cyclic voltammetry (50 mV s−1) and linear sweep voltammetry (5 mV s−1). Findings: MoS2/Mo2C achieved overpotentials of 227 mV in acidic medium and 220 mV in alkaline medium at a high current density of 1000 mA cm−2; Tafel slopes for MoS2/Mo2C were 53 mV dec−1 in acidic medium and 44 mV dec−1 in alkaline medium; The ratio of overpotential to current density (Rη/j) for MoS2/Mo2C remained small (~45 mV dec−1) at high currents, whereas Pt foil increased to >120 mV dec−1; Contact angles for 1.0 M KOH were 82.3° (Pt), 53.8° (MoS2), and ~0° (MoS2/Mo2C), indicating superior wettability for the modified catalyst; Hydrogen bubbles on MoS2/Mo2C were smaller than 0.2 mm and released easily, whereas bubbles on Pt grew to >0.5 mm and adhered firmly; XPS analysis revealed that Mo2C surfaces were modified by –OH and –O groups formed during HER, which were absent on MoS2; DFT calculations showed a hydrogen free energy of ~0.1 eV and a water dissociation energy barrier of ~0.25 eV on oxygen-terminated Mo2C surfaces; MoS2/Mo2C showed negligible shift in polarization curves after 10,000 cycles and maintained performance after 24 h at 200 mA cm−2. Mechanism: The authors propose that the MoS2/Mo2C catalyst's superior performance stems from two factors: (1) enhanced interfacial mass transfer due to micro/nano-scale roughness and surface oxygen groups that improve water affinity and bubble release, and (2) fast reaction kinetics where surface oxygen groups (–OH in acid, –O in alkali) formed on Mo2C during HER act as water dissociation promoters and facilitate hydrogen absorption/desorption. Limitations: The text notes that while the catalyst works well at high current densities, many nonprecious catalysts and even Pt/C operate well only at low current densities (e.g., 10 mA cm−2) with large overpotentials at high densities; the study focuses on three specific model catalysts and does not test other pH conditions beyond acidic, neutral, and 6 M KOH. Future work: The authors suggest that the discovery of oxygen-terminated β-Mo2C for promoting water dissociation can be used to design other HER electrocatalysts that work well in both acidic and alkaline media, and that this strategy could be further developed to design even better electrocatalysts than MoS2/Mo2C. Quote: "low overpotentials of 227 mV in acidic medium and 220 mV in alkaline medium at a high current density of 1000 mA cm−2"

card: Paper card. Question: How can the electronic structure of RuO2 be tuned to increase oxygen vacancy formation energy, thereby preventing over-oxidation and dissolution of Ru in acidic electrolytes while maintaining high OER activity?. System: WmErnRu1−m−nO2−δ nanosheets, specifically the representative W0.2Er0.1Ru0.7O2−δ composition. Processing: Hydrothermal synthesis using ruthenium(III) acetate, WCl6, ErCl3, EDTA, and citric acid in ultra-pure water at pH 9, followed by heating at 353 K for 12 h, then calcination at 573 K for 4 h and 673 K for 2 h with a heating rate of 5 K/min. Test conditions: 0.5 M H2SO4 electrolyte for LSV and stability tests at 10 mA cm−2; PEM device test at 100 mA cm−2; XPS, ESR, and ICP-MS analysis before and after 500 h stability test. Findings: The representative W0.2Er0.1Ru0.7O2−δ required a super-low overpotential of 168 mV to achieve 10 mA cm−2.; The catalyst exhibited a record stability of 500 h in 0.5 M H2SO4 electrolyte with a tiny overpotential increase of 5 mV from 250 to 500 h.; The material operated steadily for 120 h at a high current of 100 mA cm−2 in an acidic PEM device.; DFT calculations showed the O 2p band center shifted from −3.31 eV in RuO2 to −4.12 eV in the co-doped sample.; The energy for oxygen vacancy (VO) formation increased from 0.67 eV in RuO2 to 2.29 eV in W0.2Er0.1Ru0.7O2−δ.; ICP-MS analysis revealed Ru cation concentration in the solution was <12 ppb after 500 h of stability testing.; The charge-transfer resistance (Rct) for W0.2Er0.1Ru0.7O2−δ was 3.3 Ω, significantly lower than 50.8 Ω for C-RuO2.; ESR spectra showed no obvious peaks around 3275 G after the stability test, confirming no generation of oxygen vacancies.. Mechanism: Co-doping with W and Er down-shifts the O 2p band centers and enlarges the gap between the O 2p band center and the Fermi level, which decreases Ru–O bond covalency. This thermodynamically suppresses the formation of oxygen vacancies (VO) and prohibits the direct O–O coupling from lattice oxygen, thereby preventing the over-oxidation of Ru to soluble Rux>4 (e.g., RuO4). During operation, charge redistribution occurs where partial electrons transfer from W and Er to Ru, maintaining Ru in the Ru4+ state without generating soluble high-valence derivatives.. Limitations: The text does not explicitly state limitations of the study; however, it notes that solvation was not considered in the DFT calculations to understand trends when doping the RuO2 surface with foreign metal atoms.. Future work: The authors state that tuning the electronic structure of RuO2 to prevent over-oxidation opens a feasible route to keep Ru4+ active sites for acidic OER and provides a strategy to promote activity and stability by fixing catalysts, but do not explicitly list future work.. Quote: "Herein we demonstrated rationally tuning electronic structure of RuO2 with introducing W and Er, which significantly increased oxygen vacancy formation energy."

card: Paper card. Question: Can a noble metal-free high entropy glycerate (HEG) composed of five transition metals exhibit superior oxygen evolution reaction (OER) activity and stability compared to its binary, ternary, and quaternary subsystems?. System: FeNiCoCrMn glycerate (HEG) and its subsystems (binary FeNi-G, ternary FeNiCo-G, quaternary FeNiCoCr-G, FeNiCoMn-G, FeCoCrMn-G, FeNiCrMn-G, FeNiCoMn-G, NiCoCrMn-G; unary Fe-G, Ni-G, Co-G). Processing: Solvothermal synthesis: equimolar metal nitrates (0.5 mmol each of Co, Cr, Fe, Mn, Ni) dissolved in isopropanol (34 mL), mixed with glycerol (6 mL), heated in a Teflon-lined autoclave at 150 °C for 10 h, followed by centrifugation, washing with ethanol, and vacuum drying at 60 °C for 24 h. Test conditions: 1 m KOH electrolyte; three-electrode system; LSV sweep rate 5 mV s⁻¹; 80% IR compensation; cyclic voltammetry at 100 mV s⁻¹ for 3000 cycles; chronopotentiometry for 36 h at 10 and 100 mA cm⁻²; two-electrode electrolyzer for overall water splitting. Findings: HEG requires an overpotential of 229 mV to achieve 10 mA cm⁻², outperforming all subsystems.; At 100 mA cm⁻², HEG exhibits the lowest overpotential of 278 mV among all tested glycerates.; HEG displays the lowest Tafel slope of 40 mV dec⁻¹, indicating superior reaction kinetics compared to subsystems (e.g., FeNi-G at 75 mV dec⁻¹).; HEG maintains increased OER activity after 3000 CV cycles, whereas binary, ternary, and quaternary glycerates show decreased activity after 2000 cycles.; The HEG electrolyzer achieves a cell voltage of 1.63 V to reach 10 mA cm⁻² for overall water splitting.; HEG microspheres transform into a porous, amorphous sheet-like structure after OER testing, with uniform metal distribution.; The high entropy configuration results in the highest added high oxidation-state fraction (HOF) and the lowest charge transfer resistance (R_ct).; Removal of Fe from the HEG leads to the worst performance among quaternary subsystems, confirming Fe's critical role.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the enhanced OER activity to synergistic effects where multiple metals modify the electronic structure (increasing Ni³⁺ and Fe³⁺ concentrations) and coordination environment (higher HOF leading to more O—H bonds). The presence of Cr induces strain that weakens chemisorption at active sites. The high entropy configuration promotes amorphization, which provides more active sites with random orientations and unsaturated electronic configurations, accelerating charge transfer. The stability is ascribed to the high entropy configuration effect, which maintains structural integrity during cycling.. Limitations: The text notes that the exact mechanism for the decrease in charge transfer resistance (R_ct) with M—OH bonding is unknown. It also states that without optimizing the high entropy configuration, the performance is comparable to other reported materials, implying room for further tuning.. Future work: The authors propose that further modification of the FeNiCoCrMn-G HEG by adjusting the concentration and/or addition of more metals would lead to optimized glycerates exhibiting superior OER and overall water splitting activities.. Quote: "The HEG consists of 5 different metals of Fe, Ni, Co, Cr, and Mn."

card: Paper card. Question: Do high-entropy alloys (HEAs) exhibit superior electrocatalytic stability compared to lower-order alloys and pure metals due to thermodynamic contributions (configurational entropy), or are kinetic effects dominant?. System: Equiatomic thin films and carbon-supported nanoparticles of Pt, PtRu (binary), PtRuIr (ternary), PtRuIrRh (quaternary), and PtRuIrRhPd (quinary HEA); also pure elemental targets (Pt, Ru, Ir, Rh, Pd).. Processing: Thin films synthesized via magnetron co-sputtering (Ar pressure 0.667 Pa, substrate rotation 10 rpm, ~100 nm thickness); Carbon-supported nanoparticles synthesized via carbothermal shock synthesis (flash heating/cooling ~10^4 K s^-1, hold at ~2,000 K for 1,000 ms, 20 wt% metal loading).. Test conditions: Electrochemical protocols in 0.1 M HClO4 (acidic) and 0.05 M KOH (alkaline) media; Potential windows covering HER, ORR, and OER (0.05 to 1.5 VRHE); Protocols included cyclic voltammetry (scan rate 5 mV s^-1, upper potential limits 0.9, 1.2, 1.5 VRHE) and potentiostatic holds (1.2 VRHE for 10 min, 0.05 VRHE for 5 min).. Findings: Dissolved amounts for all metals generally decreased with the increasing number of alloy constituents, primarily scaling with the decreasing molar fraction of the specific element in the alloy.; In alkaline media, normalized dissolved amounts (NDA) for Pt, Ru, and Ir in the quinary HEA were significantly lower than in pure metals; Ru NDA dropped by two orders of magnitude at 1.5 VRHE.; In acidic media, while absolute dissolved amounts decreased, normalized dissolved amounts (NDA) for most elements were higher or similar to pure metals, indicating no thermodynamic stability enhancement.; Carbon-supported nanoparticles showed similar dissolution trends to thin films but with significantly higher noise and higher absolute dissolution rates due to larger surface area.; The onset potential of dissolution for each metal did not visibly change with the number of elements in the alloy.; Ru was stabilized already in the binary alloy (PtRu), with dissolution monotonically decreasing as Ir, Rh, and Pd were added, especially in alkaline media.; No striking improvement in stability was observed for Rh and Pd in the HEA compared to their pure counterparts in either acidic or alkaline media.. Mechanism: The authors argue that the observed stability improvements are due to dissolution kinetic effects overcompensating thermodynamic contributions, and that the reduction in dissolution is explained by the lowered concentration of elements in multinary alloys rather than synergistic effects of configurational entropy.. Limitations: The study notes that the improvement in stability under alkaline conditions was not striking and that the data for carbon-supported nanoparticles was noisier, potentially masking subtle differences in normalized dissolved amounts.. Future work: The authors suggest that while thin films are excellent for fundamental studies, once behavior is mapped, systems closer to real applications (like NPs) should be studied, and that a detailed mechanistic picture of HEA dissolution is currently impossible due to the dynamic surface composition.. Quote: "We postulate that this is because of dissolution kinetic effects, which are always present under electrocatalytic conditions, overcompensating thermodynamic contributions."

Paper card. Question: How does alloy composition and the presence of specific elements affect the stability and dissolution behavior of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) and binary alloys under electrocatalytic conditions, and can stability be tuned by regulating the amount of a more stable element?. System: PtRuIrRhPd (equimolar, 20% molar fraction each), Pt-rich binary (Pt:Ru 4:1), Ru-rich binary (Pt:Ru 1:4), and constituent single metals (Pt, Ru, Ir, Rh, Pd). Processing: Sputtered thin films deposited via ultra-high vacuum PVD (CMS 400/600 LIN) at 25°C, 0.67 Pa Ar pressure, 60 sccm flow, resulting in ~100 nm thickness; Carbon-supported nanoparticles synthesized via carbothermal shock (Joule-heated to ~2000 K for ~1 s) from metal salt/ethanol precursors on carbon black (20 wt% loading). Test conditions: Electrochemical protocols in 0.1 M HClO4 and 0.05 M KOH; Potentiostatic holds at 0.05 VRHE (5 min) and 1.2 VRHE (10 min); RDE measurements with 200 mV s⁻¹ scan rate; On-line ICP-MS for dissolution quantification. Findings: The highest cumulative dissolution was measured for the HEA sample (PtRuIrRhPd) in acid.; Cumulative dissolution is significantly higher for the Ru-rich binary alloy (Pt:Ru 1:4) than the Pt-rich alloy (Pt:Ru 4:1) regardless of the chemical environment.; Cumulative dissolution of the HEA sample is comparable to the one obtained for the Pt-rich binary alloy in alkaline media.; Regulating the amount of the element with relatively higher stability (Pt) allows tuning of the resulting alloy's stability.; Only one or two elements may be active toward the given electrocatalytic reaction instead of all alloy constituents.; The study investigated only equimolar compositions (20 at% for each element) rather than the whole composition space.; On-line ICP-MS successfully measured dissolved metal ions for HEA samples and is integrable in closed-loop autonomous workflows.. Mechanism: The authors argue that thermodynamic contributions are highest in equimolar compositions, which should theoretically bear the highest stability, but observed dissolution is heavily influenced by the specific stability of individual constituents (e.g., Pt vs. Ru) and the electrocatalytic environment (pH, potential). They suggest that stability changes may result from a decrease in the amount of metal or additional stabilization phenomena (thermodynamic or kinetic), and that activity and stability must be interpreted together to rule out inactive elements.. Limitations: The main limitation is that only equimolar compositions were investigated instead of the whole composition space due to the use of a traditional experimental workflow without high-throughput/autonomous tools. Additionally, conclusions only apply to the specific system PtRuIrRhPd with exactly 20% molar fractions of each constituent.. Future work: Future efforts will focus on performing similar experiments in an autonomous workflow by integrating high-throughput toolkit elements into the on-line ICP-MS setup to rapidly screen the entire composition space. The authors also propose shifting from heuristic to Bayesian approaches (e.g., genetic algorithms) to decrease the number of experiments and refine theoretical models for predicting multinary electrocatalyst stability.. Quote: "The highest cumulative dissolution was measured for the HEA sample in acid."

Test conditions: HER tested in N2-saturated 1 M KOH (LSV scan rate 5 mV s−1, stability via chronoamperometry at 11 mV and 10,000 CV cycles); MOR tested in N2-saturated 1 M KOH + 1 M CH3OH (CV scan rate 20 mV s−1, stability via chronoamperometry at 0.65 V and 1,000 CV cycles).. Findings: The Pt18Ni26Fe15Co14Cu27/C catalyst exhibits an ultrasmall overpotential of 11 mV at a current density of 10 mA cm−2 for HER, compared to 84 mV for commercial Pt/C.; The mass activity for HER is 10.96 A mg−1Pt at −0.07 V vs. RHE, significantly higher than the 0.83 A mg−1Pt of commercial Pt/C.; The catalyst achieves a mass activity of 15.04 A mg−1Pt for MOR, which is 10 times higher than that of Pt/C (1.45 A mg−1Pt).; The catalyst maintains 99% of its current density after 10 hours of chronoamperometry at 11 mV, whereas Pt/C retains only ~53%.; After 10,000 CV cycles, the Pt18Ni26Fe15Co14Cu27/C catalyst shows no obvious negative shift in overpotential, while Pt/C shifts by ~33 mV.; The Tafel slope for HER is 30 mV dec−1 for the HEA catalyst compared to 98 mV dec−1 for Pt/C, indicating faster kinetics.; CO stripping onset potential is 0.391 V vs. RHE for the HEA catalyst, a 181 mV decrease compared to Pt/C (0.572 V), indicating superior CO anti-poisoning.; DFT calculations reveal a low activation barrier of 0.11 eV for water dissociation and a rate-determining step energy barrier of 0.45 eV for MOR.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the performance to a synergistic effect of multi-active sites on the HEA surface, where different elements (Pt, Ni, Fe, Co, Cu) facilitate specific steps: Pt acts as an electron reservoir, Ni and Co dominate the electroactive region near the Fermi level for electron depletion, and Fe stabilizes intermediates. This configuration enables fast site-to-site electron transfer, efficient water dissociation, and optimal binding strength for intermediates, while the lattice distortion and multi-component nature inhibit CO poisoning and structural degradation.. Limitations: The text notes that slight stoichiometry variations (e.g., changing Cu content) lead to slightly lower activity, though the optimal composition is robust; it also mentions that non-noble metals (Ni, Fe, Co, Cu) may leach slightly during electrocatalysis, causing minor stoichiometry variations, although the overall structure remains stable.. Future work: The authors propose that the simple oil phase synthesis strategy and the understanding of the multi-active sites and fast site-to-site electron transfer mechanism will lay the foundation for the preparation of other HEAs and their application in related electrocatalysis.. card: Paper card. Question: How can high-entropy materials (HEMs) leverage configurational entropy to overcome the limitations of conventional enthalpy-dominated catalysts, specifically regarding phase stability, active site tunability, and the breaking of scaling relationships in electrocatalysis?. System: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) including PtPdCoNiFeCuAuSn, PtPdRhRuCe, Ru0.44Rh0.30Co0.12Ni0.14, CoxMoyFe10Ni10Cu10, IrPdPtRhRu, Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni, and AlNiCoIrM; High-entropy oxides (HEOs) and perovskites; Multimetallic nanoclusters (MMNCs).. Processing: Carbothermal shock (ultrafast joule heating followed by rapid quenching at ~1500 K); Fast moving bed pyrolysis (FMBP) reaching 923 K within 5 s; Colloidal synthesis with seed-mediated coreduction and annealing at 600°C; Ionic liquid-assisted cosputtering; Ball milling and solvothermal synthesis.. Test conditions: Ammonia oxidation at 700°C; Ammonia decomposition at 500°C; Oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) in acidic and alkaline media; Oxygen evolution reaction (OER) in acidic and alkaline media; Hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) in acidic and alkaline solutions; Li-O2 battery cycling.. Findings: Quinary HEA nanoparticles (PtPdRhRuCe) achieved ~100% conversion and >99% selectivity toward NO + NO2 at 700°C with no degradation over 30 hours.; HEA-Co25Mo45 catalyst reached a mass-specific rate of 0.74 gNH3 m−2 hour−1 at 500°C, representing improvement factors of ~24 versus bimetallic Co-Mo and ~19 versus Ru.; Computational models predicted an IrPdPtRhRu HEA composition with a ~40-mV lower overpotential relative to Pt (111) for ORR.; Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni nanoparticles with size less than 2 nm delivered ORR activity comparable to Pt under the same conditions.; Octonary RuIrCeNiWCuCrCo catalyst outperformed quaternary and binary counterparts in long-term operation for Li-O2 batteries due to higher configurational entropy.; GO-supported quinary HEA nanoparticles (FeCoPdIrPt) exhibited enhanced HER activity and stability in alkaline solutions relative to commercial Pt/C catalysts.; HEA catalysts containing five or more elements outperformed binary, ternary, and quaternary alloys in alkaline media due to broad adsorption energy distributions.. Mechanism: Enhanced configurational entropy stabilizes single-phase solid solutions despite large enthalpic differences, allowing atomic mixing of multiple principal elements. Severe lattice distortion lowers the energy barrier for adsorption and activation, while the diverse local coordination environments and electronic perturbations (ligand effects) create a near-continuum distribution of adsorption energies. This distribution allows the catalyst to access optimal binding strengths for intermediates, breaking the linear scaling relationships that limit conventional catalysts.. Limitations: Low surface area of bulk HEAs limits catalytic utilization; maintaining nanoscale morphology at elevated temperatures is difficult due to migration and aggregation; synthesis of single-phase HEAs requires overcoming thermodynamic barriers; characterization is challenging due to increased compositional and structural complexities; phase segregation can occur if entropy is insufficient to overcome enthalpic differences.. Future work: Further elucidation of structure-property relationships across different HEM subcategories; development of high-throughput synthesis and measurement tools for accelerated materials discovery; deeper mechanistic studies on surface restructuring under reaction conditions; optimization of catalyst stability for noble metal-free applications.. Quote: "The ability to confine multiple principal elements in a single lattice is intriguing for the design of advanced catalysts with desirable activity, selectivity, and stability."

Paper card. Question: How can the configurational entropy in high-entropy alloys (HEAs) be leveraged to overcome the miscibility limitations of traditional alloys and enhance catalytic performance for complex reactions like ethanol oxidation?. System: Platinum-group metal (PGM) high-entropy alloy (HEA) nanoparticles containing Ru, Rh, Pd, Os, Ir, and Pt; specifically compared against physical mixtures of unary PGMs and binary/ternary/quaternary/quinary PGM alloys.. Processing: Prepared using a facile polyol method to synthesize PGM-HEA nanoparticles.. Test conditions: Electrochemical ethanol oxidation reaction in aqueous solution; performance compared against commercial Pd/C, Pd black, Pt/C, and Au@PtIr/C catalysts; cyclic voltammetry used to analyze individual constituent contributions.. Findings: The PGM-HEA nanoparticles exhibited much higher activity relative to commercial Pd/C, Pd black, and Pt/C catalysts.; Negligible activity was observed for the physical mixture of the six unary PGM nanoparticles, confirming the necessity of atomic mixing.; The PGM-HEA delivered a mass activity more than 1.5 times higher than that of the most active catalyst to date (Au@PtIr/C).; The PGM-HEA exhibited the highest current density in the full potential range compared to ternary, quaternary, and quinary PGM alloys.; Pt and Pd are active for ethanol conversion but become poisoned by adsorbed (CO)ad or CHx species.; Os and Ru facilitate the oxidation of (CO)ad, mitigating the poisoning effect for Pt and Pd.; Ir and Ru ensure that dehydrogenation or C─C cleavage occurs at a low potential, while further oxidation hinges on Pt and Pd components.. Mechanism: The atomically mixed metals in HEAs play distinct yet concerted functions: Pt and Pd drive ethanol conversion; Os and Ru mitigate poisoning by oxidizing adsorbed species; Ir and Ru lower the potential for C─C cleavage and dehydrogenation. This synergy allows for efficient and complete oxidation of ethanol involving multiple proton-electron transfers.. Limitations: The text notes that while simple reactions can be triggered by mono- and bimetallic PGMs, it is difficult to drive complex reactions involving multiple proton-electron transfers and intermediate species without the synergistic effects provided by HEAs.. Future work: The authors imply the need to better understand the contribution of each metal to the overall reaction, as demonstrated by their comparison of cyclic voltammetry curves of individual constituents to elucidate specific roles in preventing poisoning and facilitating cleavage.. Quote: "The PGM-HEA nanoparticles efficiently catalyzed the ethanol oxidation reaction, exhibiting a much higher activity relative to that of the commercial Pd/C, Pd black, and Pt/C catalysts, respectively."
W3162678041.title: High-entropy materials for catalysis: A new frontier

card: Paper card. Question: How do the unique structural features of compositionally complex solid solutions (CCSS) enable new concepts in electrocatalyst design compared to traditional catalysts, and what are the strategies to exploit these features for activity, selectivity, and stability?. System: Compositionally complex solid solutions (CCSS) and high-entropy alloys (HEAs) defined as single-phase solid solutions with five or more elements, including specific examples like Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni and Pd-based systems.. Processing: Synthesis via entropy-driven routes at high temperatures or high energies to ensure negative Gibbs free energy; non-equilibrium methods such as fast cooling rates (quenching) to kinetically trap metastable phases or achieve high deviations from equiatomic compositions (e.g., 60–70% of one element).. Test conditions: Electrochemical reactions including oxygen reduction reaction (ORR), oxygen evolution reaction (OER), hydrogen evolution reaction (HER), CO oxidation, CO reduction, CO2 reduction, NH3 synthesis/decomposition, MeOH oxidation, EtOH oxidation, and Li-O2 batteries.. Findings: CCSS materials form a single-phase solid solution where all elements are statistically distributed, creating millions of different multielement active sites with a continuous distribution of binding energies.; The binding energy distribution pattern (BEDP) for a quinary alloy shows at least five distinct binding peaks, with the position of the peak maximum related to overpotential and the integral related to the number of active sites.; Increasing the molar ratio of a specific element can increase the number of sites within a binding peak to about 60–70%, significantly surpassing the loss of site probability compared to unary catalysts.; In CCSS surfaces, the scaling relation between *O and *OH/*OOH is broken because *O binds at threefold hollow sites while *OH and *OOH bind at on-top sites with different elemental compositions.; For cascade reactions like CO2 reduction, the multifunctionality allows intermediate products to desorb and re-bind at different sites, enabling the synthesis of higher-carbon products.; The thermodynamic stability of the CCSS phase is counterbalanced by kinetic stabilization due to sluggish diffusion and high solid diffusion barriers, leading to high electrocatalytic stability.; The position of individual elements in standard volcano plots is not decisive; for example, Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni showed good ORR activity even though all individual elements are far from optimal volcano positions.. Mechanism: The authors argue that the immense flexibility in adjusting binding energies arises because every active site has a different elemental environment due to the statistical distribution of elements. This creates a continuous coverage of binding energies via BEDP peak broadening, allowing the formation of sites with ideal binding energies. Additionally, the unique multifunctionality allows different reaction steps or intermediates to bind at different sites, breaking traditional scaling relations and enabling cascade reactions.. Limitations: A lower abundance of relevant active sites on the surface compared to unary catalysts; the complexity of predicting suitable element combinations due to multielement interactions; challenges in synthesizing particles with controlled composition, size, and morphology; and the potential for thermodynamic degradation if the CCSS phase is metastable.. Future work: The authors propose developing a database summarizing calculated and experimental data, implementing high-throughput methods, using machine learning tools to identify trends in the complex composition space, and designing synthesis routes that allow upscaling to industrial scale while controlling electrochemical properties.. Quote: "Since the binding energy is a result of many short‐range and long‐range interactions of the binding atom(s) with all neighbouring atoms, an active site can consist of any possible arrangement of the constituent elements."

card: Paper card. Question: How does thermal shock (annealing at 400–800 °C) affect the microstructure, mechanical properties, and tribocorrosion resistance of strongly amorphous AlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy films in extreme service environments?. System: AlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy film (composition: 15.82 at.% Al, 22.86 at.% Cr, 19.49 at.% Ti, 24.74 at.% Zr, 17.09 at.% Mo) deposited on 304 stainless steel and silicon wafers. Processing: Co-filter cathode vacuum arc deposition (Co-FCVAD) using Ti50Mo50, pure Al, Cr, and Zr targets; substrate sputtered at −800, −600, and −400 V for 45 s; annealed in air at 400 °C, 600 °C, and 800 °C for 1 h. Test conditions: High-temperature oxidation in air at 800 °C for 1 h; tribocorrosion in 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution with Si3N4 ceramic balls (Φ 6 mm) at 5 N load, 1 Hz frequency for 50 min (10–40 min loading phase). Findings: After annealing at 800 °C for 1 h, a dense ZrTiO4 composite oxide layer formed with a thickness of 5.47 μm and oxygen content of 20.50 at.%; Hardness (H) and Young's modulus (E) reached maximum values of 20.88 GPa and 220.2 GPa, respectively, after annealing at 800 °C; The H/E ratio and H3/E2 ratio for the 800 °C annealed film were 0.0948 and 0.1877, respectively, indicating superior crack and plastic deformation resistance; The film annealed at 800 °C exhibited the lowest tribocorrosion metrics: ΔOCP = 0.055, COF = 0.04, and wear rate = 1.34 × 10−6 mm−3·N−1·m−1; Annealing at 400 °C and 600 °C resulted in no oxide particles and minimal changes in film thickness or morphology; The amorphous structure at 600 °C led to increased hardness (14.97 GPa) and modulus (176.1 GPa) due to relaxation, while 800 °C added dispersion strengthening from oxide precipitates. Mechanism: Zr and Ti elements preferentially oxidize to form ZrO2 and TiO2; competitive oxidation-reduction reactions occur where TiO2 is reduced by Zr, leading to the accumulation of oxides that polymerize into stable ZrTiO4 spinel; this dense composite oxide layer acts as a barrier preventing further oxidation, while the fine oxide particles provide dispersion strengthening to enhance mechanical properties and tribocorrosion resistance.. Quote: "the formation of a dense ZrTiO4 composite oxide layer on the surface actively prevents the oxidation from continuing"

card: Paper card. Question: How can a nanocrystalline refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) film with superior mechanical and tribological properties be synthesized using a cost-effective single consolidated target, and what are the effects of annealing on its adhesion and wear resistance?. System: Equimolar CuMoTaWV refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) film deposited on silicon and 304 stainless-steel substrates. Processing: DC-magnetron sputtering using a single target prepared by partial spark plasma sintering (SPS) of equimolar elemental powders (Cu, Mo, Ta, W, V) at 1000 °C under 40 MPa pressure; film deposition at 500 °C substrate temperature for 120 min; annealing at 300 °C for adhesion improvement. Test conditions: Nanoindentation at 3 mN load; nanopillar compression (440 nm diameter) with max force 3 mN; tribological wear tests at room temperature (RT) and 300 °C using 1 N load and 0.1 m/s sliding speed against E52100 alloy steel counterballs. Findings: The as-deposited film exhibited a nanocrystalline body-centered cubic (BCC) solid solution with an average grain size of 18 nm and a thickness of ~900 nm.; Nanoindentation yielded an average hardness of 19 ± 2.3 GPa and an elastic modulus of 259 ± 19.2 GPa.; Nanopillar compression tests revealed a high compressive strength of 10 ± 0.8 GPa (yield strength 10.7 ± 0.8 GPa).; Annealing at 300 °C reduced surface roughness to 2 nm (Sa) and significantly improved film adhesion compared to the as-deposited state.; The annealed film showed an average coefficient of friction (COF) of 0.25 at RT and 1.5 at 300 °C.; Wear rates were 6.4 × 10⁻⁶ mm³/N m at RT and 2.5 × 10⁻⁵ mm³/N m at 300 °C, which are 10² times lower than 304 stainless steel at RT.; The film hardness was ~20% higher than previously reported RHEA films in the literature.. Mechanism: The high hardness and strength are attributed to nanocrystalline grain size, grain boundary strengthening, solid solution hardening, lattice distortion, and sluggish diffusion. The strengthening mechanism in nanopillars shifts from dislocation-controlled to grain-boundary-controlled plastic deformation, leading to intergranular fracture. Annealing improves adhesion and stability, while the formation of CuO at 300 °C influences tribological behavior.. Limitations: The as-deposited film showed excessive plastic deformation, smearing, and radial cracks due to low adhesion, leading to a sharp increase in COF after 15 m of sliding. The film composition showed in-depth nonhomogeneity, being rich in W, Ta, and Mo at the surface and V at the interface. The high COF at 300 °C was attributed to tribochemical reactions and oxide formation on the counterball.. Future work: The study suggests that RHEA films can be beneficial for wear and nanopillar applications and may lead to processing for large-scale industrial applications.. Quote: "The nanocrystalline nature of the RHEA film resulted in a hardness of 19 ± 2.3 GPa and an elastic modulus of 259 ± 19.2 GPa."

card: Paper card. Question: How does long-term thermal exposure at 1000 °C affect the structural stability, grain growth kinetics, and mechanical properties of a TiCoCrFeMn high-entropy alloy, and what is the role of the sluggish diffusion effect in this process?. System: TiCoCrFeMn high-entropy alloy (two-phase BCC solid solution + C14 Laves phase). Processing: Powder metallurgy: mechanical alloying of Ti, Co, Cr, Fe, Mn powders (5 h, argon) followed by sintering via U-FAST (modified Spark Plasma Sintering) at 1050 °C for 1 min, then homogenization annealing at 1000 °C for up to 1000 h in argon. Test conditions: Annealing times: 1, 10, 20, 50, 100, and 1000 h at 1000 °C in argon atmosphere; microhardness measured via Vickers method (0.025–1.0 kgf); grain size analyzed via EBSD; diffusion coefficients calculated from EDS linear scans. Findings: Structural stability was achieved after 100 h of annealing, with stable grain sizes of approximately 2 µm for the BCC solid solution and 0.4 µm for the BCC+C14 mixture.; Long-term heating up to 1000 h caused grain growth to 2.7 µm (BCC) and 0.7 µm (BCC+C14), accompanied by a hardness decrease from 1065 HV to 1000 HV.; The highest grain growth rate was 0.0235 µm·h⁻¹ during the initial 10–50 h period due to non-monotonic chemical changes, while the two-phase region grew at 0.0081 µm·h⁻¹.; In the stable state (100–1000 h), grain growth slowed significantly to 0.0004–0.0007 µm·h⁻¹.; Diffusion coefficients stabilized at DCr = 1.28 × 10⁻¹⁹ m²·s⁻¹ and DTi = 1.04 × 10⁻¹⁹ m²·s⁻¹, demonstrating the sluggish diffusion effect.; The chromium diffusion coefficient in the alloy was three orders of magnitude lower than in the Ni3Al superstructure.; Non-monotonic changes in chemical composition between 10–100 h caused fluctuations in hardness and phase fractions before stabilization.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the high structural stability and slowed grain growth to the 'sluggish diffusion effect' and 'cocktail effect' typical of high-entropy alloys. The thermodynamically stable Laves C14 phase inhibits grain growth in the two-phase region, while the non-monotonic chemical composition changes during the initial 10–100 h drive phase reconstruction and mass transport, eventually leading to a stable matrix where the Hall-Petch relationship holds.. Limitations: The text notes that the presence of coagulating titanium oxide precipitates (likely from unreduced powder surfaces and air compaction) prevented precise automated grain size analysis, requiring non-automated outlining. Additionally, in the ultra-fine two-phase regions, it was impossible to distinguish individual grains belonging to the solid solution versus the intermetallic phase, so they were analyzed as a common region.. Future work: The authors state that the detailed analysis of the hardness measurement models (H-K, PSR, MPSR, N-G) and their accuracy will be discussed in a separate work devoted only to this issue.. Quote: "It was found that the tested alloy achieved structural stability after 100 h of annealing."
